prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

U0107: Figure 5: DWR Route Display Auxiliary Waypoint Return Capture Fix Maneuver Start (SWAP Route) Point (MSP) The long window at the bottom shows the current flight plan route and DWR advisory, along with time- savings for various downstream fixes at left.
U0108: This is labeled as the ‘Capture fix menu & flying time savings’ in the figure.
U0109: The two windows on the right show the sector congestion for the current flight plan route (top) and the DWR advisory (bottom).
U0110: The corresponding sector congestion values (as red or yellow sectors) for those routes are shown within.
U0111: Red sectors are those where the congestion is caused by aircraft that are all currently airborne, while yellow sectors have proposed departure aircraft causing predicted congestion.
U0112: This allows DWR users to visualize proposed routes and modify them if necessary using point, click, and drag inputs.
U0113: Users can adjust the RCF, the number and position of auxiliary waypoints, and the MSP through interactive points, click, and drag actions if needed.
U0114: Metrics, including flight time savings (or delay), proximity to current and forecast weather, downstream sector congestion, traffic conflicts, and SUA conflicts, all update dynamically as the user modifies a proposed route.
U0115: Conflicts with weather or traffic cause DWR to dismiss a potential reroute (trial plan) and keep searching for another (see Figure 6).
U0116: Figure 6: Example of trial plan with weather and traffic conflicts that would prevent DWR from suggesting this route.
U0117: Research indicates that digital communication of proposed DWR routes between ATC and the flight deck combined with on-board display of proposed route, would allow much faster review and approval of the DWR route [4] [5]. 4.1 CONVECTIVE WEATHER MODEL DWR utilizes convective weather forecast data from FAA’s Corridor Integrated Weather System (CIWS) and Convective Weather Avoidance Model (CWAM) [15-17] to identify routes that will avoid convective cells.
U0118: CIWS forecasts the growth, decay, and movement of convective weather and updates every 5 minutes with a 2-hour look-ahead time in 5-minute increments (see Figure 7).
U0119: This allows DWR to identify alternative routes that are predicted to remain clear of weather at the time the flight is calculated to pass the cell(s).
U0120: Figure 7: CIWS and CWAM Forecast Sample Figure 8: CIWS cell and corresponding 60, 70, & 80% CWAM polygons CWAM identifies boundaries around convective cells that represent the distance by which flight crews are expected to deviate around the cell [15][16][17].
U0121: The boundary polygon, known as a Weather Avoidance Field (WAF), represents the probability a flight crew will deviate around the cell based on storm intensity, echo tops, and look-ahead time.
U0122: A WAF is identified by the probability that a given percentage of pilots would deviate around the storm at that distance based on extensive historical data.
U0123: For a given weather cell and altitude, 70% of WAF polygons are generally smaller with their boundaries closer to the weather cells than are 60% WAF polygons (see Figure 8).
U0124: WAF polygons (60, 70, and 80%) are identified for every 5-minute CWIS forecast interval out to 2 hours, at flight levels ranging from FL250 to FL450 in 1,000’ increments.
U0125: DWR normally utilizes 70% WAF polygons when generating route advisories, but the default WAF parameter can be selected at system start up. 4.2 CONVECTIVE CELL GAP DETECTION AND REJECTION DWR logic includes gap detection and rejection logic to ensure a gap is large enough to safely route aircraft.
U0126: This function includes a distance buffer that will reject a route amendment if it will go through a gap that is narrower than 50nm laterally (user-adjustable parameter) either side of route and 75nm longitudinally (user-adjustable parameter) to the predicted cells at the time the aircraft reaches the point closest to the cells (see Figure 9).
U0127: If convective cells are predicted to encroach on one side of a trajectory but not on the other, (blue polygons in left graphic of Figure 9) it is generally not considered an operational problem because there is room for flight crews to maneuver around the cell.
